questions.stem: A 45 year old office worker has 5 months of hard, pellet-like stools every 4 to 5 days, with straining and a feeling of incomplete emptying. She has no abdominal pain, bleeding or weight loss. She eats little fruit or vegetables. Her abdomen feels full with palpable stool in the left iliac fossa, and rectal examination shows hard stool.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Infrequent hard stools with straining and incomplete evacuation, a low-fibre diet, palpable stool and normal bloods with no red flags is simple functional constipation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: hard, pellet-like stools every 4 to 5 days
steps.x: Constipation is hard stools, straining, infrequency or incomplete evacuation; no pain rules out IBS.

elim: There are no red flags: no bleeding, weight loss or anaemia, and she is 45.
Hirschsprung's presents from birth with delayed meconium.
Her TSH is normal.
IBS needs abdominal pain related to defecation, which she does not have.

steps.x: B: Functional constipation. Low fibre, low fluids and immobility are the commonest causes.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with diabetic neuropathy started a new medicine for burning foot pain 6 weeks ago. Since then she has had a dry mouth, blurred vision and hard stools every 4 days. She also takes metformin, ramipril and atorvastatin, all unchanged for years.
questions.q: Which medicine is most likely to have caused her constipation?
questions.e: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic with anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, blurred vision and constipation from reduced parasympathetic drive to gut smooth muscle.

steps.x: The question asks: Which medicine is most likely to have caused her constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
New neuropathic pain drug plus anticholinergic side effects = amitriptyline.

elim: She has taken it unchanged for years and statins do not typically constipate.
Metformin causes diarrhoea, not constipation.
ACE inhibitors cause cough, not constipation.
SSRIs more often loosen stools and she was not started on it.

steps.x: A: Amitriptyline. Drug causes: anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers, opioids, iron.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman is 8 weeks after delivering her first baby. She was found to be anaemic after a postpartum haemorrhage and started a new tablet. She now has hard, dark stools and strains to pass them. She is breastfeeding and has no abdominal pain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her constipation?
questions.e: Oral iron, started for postpartum anaemia, commonly causes constipation and dark stools.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Anaemia treatment plus dark hard stools = oral iron.

elim: Folic acid does not cause constipation.
NSAIDs cause dyspepsia, not constipation.
Lactulose treats constipation.
Paracetamol does not slow the bowel.

steps.x: A: Ferrous sulfate. Iron tablets are a common, easily missed drug cause of constipation.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has 2 years of worsening constipation. He has a resting tremor of his right hand, slowness of movement, a shuffling gait and a reduced facial expression. His TSH, calcium and haemoglobin are normal and colonoscopy last year was normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his constipation?
questions.e: Resting tremor, bradykinesia and shuffling gait point to Parkinson's disease, a neurological secondary cause of constipation through autonomic involvement of the gut.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Look for the secondary cause: endocrine, structural or neurological.

elim: A normal colonoscopy and 2-year course make this unlikely.
His calcium is normal.
His TSH is normal.
There are no leg weakness or sensory signs.

steps.x: D: Parkinson's disease. Secondary causes: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, colorectal cancer or stricture, Parkinson's, spinal cord disease.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has chronic constipation and strains to pass hard stools. For 3 weeks he has had severe, sharp pain on opening his bowels that lasts for an hour, with a streak of bright red blood on the paper. Examination of the anus is very painful.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Thrombosed purple lump at the anal margin
questions.e: Tearing pain on defecation with bright red blood after passing hard stools is an anal fissure, a complication of constipation, usually in the posterior midline.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: severe, sharp pain on opening his bowels
steps.x: Hard stools tear the anoderm; the commonest site is posterior midline.

elim: A mass suggests cancer, which does not cause this sharp pain in a young man.
Prolapsing haemorrhoids are usually painless.
That is a perianal abscess, with constant pain and fever.
A thrombosed haemorrhoid gives constant pain, not pain on defecation only.

steps.x: D: Posterior midline anal tear. Complications of constipation: anal fissure, haemorrhoids, impaction, overflow diarrhoea.

questions.stem: An 89 year old woman in a care home has 4 days of foul-smelling watery stool leaking several times a day, after not opening her bowels for 10 days. She is bed-bound after a stroke and takes codeine. Her temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 80 bpm. Her abdomen is mildly distended with palpable stool.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on digital rectal examination?
o: Fresh red blood on the glove
questions.e: Watery leakage after days without a bowel motion in an immobile patient on codeine is overflow diarrhoea: liquid stool leaks around a hard impacted mass felt on DRE.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on digital rectal examination? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: not opening her bowels for 10 days
steps.x: Diarrhoea after constipation in an immobile elderly patient is impaction until the DRE says otherwise.

elim: An empty rectum would point away from impaction.
There is no history of bleeding.
A tumour is possible in the elderly but the history is classic impaction.
She is a woman; this would suggest prostatitis in a man.

steps.x: D: Rectum loaded with hard stool. Overflow diarrhoea reflects faecal impaction and is treated as impaction, not diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has had constipation all his life. His mother says he did not pass meconium until day 4 after a term birth. He has episodes of marked abdominal distension that settle with enemas. He is thin. A contrast study and colonoscopy show no structural lesion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lifelong constipation from birth, meconium delayed beyond 48 hours in a term baby and intermittent pseudo-obstruction with no structural lesion is Hirschsprung's disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: did not pass meconium until day 4
steps.x: Delayed meconium in a term baby is the key clue.

elim: A fissure gives painful defecation, not lifelong constipation from birth.
Coeliac disease does not delay meconium.
Functional constipation does not start with delayed meconium.
Congenital hypothyroidism is picked up on newborn screening and causes other features.

steps.x: D: Hirschsprung's disease. Hirschsprung's: delayed meconium (over 48 h), lifelong constipation, pseudo-obstruction.

questions.stem: A 2 day old term baby boy has not passed meconium. He is feeding poorly and his abdomen is distended. Digital rectal examination is performed by the paediatric registrar. Hirschsprung's disease is suspected.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding as the finger is withdrawn?
o: Explosive release of stool and gas
Hard impacted stool in a dilated rectum
Normal rectal tone with no stool release
questions.e: In Hirschsprung's disease the aganglionic rectum is tight and empty; withdrawing the finger releases the obstruction, giving an explosive gush of stool and gas.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding as the finger is withdrawn? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
A tight empty rectum then a gush is the classic Hirschsprung's DRE.

elim: Redcurrant-jelly stool suggests intussusception.
In Hirschsprung's the rectum is narrow and empty.
Imperforate anus would be seen at birth and prevents DRE.
This would make Hirschsprung's less likely.

steps.x: B: Explosive release of stool and gas. Consider Hirschsprung's in any term neonate without meconium by 48 hours.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is 4 days after a knee replacement. He is taking oxycodone, paracetamol, enoxaparin and his usual omeprazole. He has not opened his bowels since surgery and feels bloated. His abdomen is soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds.
questions.q: Which medicine is most likely responsible for his constipation?
questions.e: Opioids act on mu receptors in the enteric nervous system to reduce motility and increase fluid absorption; oxycodone is the culprit.

steps.x: The question asks: Which medicine is most likely responsible for his constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: not opened his bowels since surgery
steps.x: New opioid plus immobility after surgery = opioid-induced constipation.

elim: Low molecular weight heparin does not slow the bowel.
PPIs are not a significant cause of constipation and he took it before.
Paracetamol does not cause constipation.
Its effect has worn off within hours.

steps.x: C: Oxycodone. Opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers and iron are the key drug causes.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has had chronic constipation for years and strains hard on the toilet. She now has painless bright red blood on the paper and dripping into the pan, with a soft swelling that comes down when she strains and goes back by itself. Rectal examination is normal.
questions.q: Which complication of her constipation has she most likely developed?
questions.e: Chronic straining raises pressure in the anal cushions; painless bright red bleeding with a swelling that reduces spontaneously is grade 2 haemorrhoids.

steps.x: The question asks: Which complication of her constipation has she most likely developed? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Straining plus painless bright red blood = haemorrhoids.

elim: A fissure is painful, and this bleeding is painless.
A reducible swelling with painless bleeding in a 40 year old is more likely haemorrhoids.
Impaction does not give a prolapsing swelling.
Full-thickness prolapse is usually in older women and does not reduce itself so easily.

steps.x: D: Haemorrhoids. Complications: impaction, haemorrhoids, anal fissures, overflow diarrhoea.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman with dementia is admitted with reduced mobility after a fall. Staff note she has not opened her bowels for 9 days and drinks little. Her abdomen is distended with mild tenderness and a firm, indentable mass in the left iliac fossa. She has no vomiting and bowel sounds are present.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the mass?
questions.e: An indentable left-sided mass in an elderly, immobile, dehydrated patient who has not opened her bowels for 9 days is a palpable stool burden.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the mass? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: not opened her bowels for 9 days
steps.x: Faeces indent; tumours do not.

elim: An abscess gives fever and marked tenderness.
An ovarian mass is in the pelvis and is not indentable.
A tumour is hard and not indentable.
Volvulus gives acute obstruction with vomiting and gross distension.

steps.x: B: Faecal loading. Suspect impaction in the elderly or immobile with a palpable stool burden.

questions.stem: An 86 year old man with chronic constipation has 3 days of increasing confusion and drowsiness. He has hardly eaten or drunk and has had several episodes of vomiting stool-free fluid. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. His mucous membranes are dry.
questions.q: Which complication is most likely to explain his blood results?
questions.e: Raised urea out of proportion to creatinine, raised sodium, tachycardia and dry membranes show dehydration, a recognised complication of constipation in the elderly.

steps.x: The question asks: Which complication is most likely to explain his blood results? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
A high urea:creatinine ratio with tachycardia means he is dry.

elim: His calcium is normal.
His TSH is normal.
There is no fever or source of infection described.
SIADH gives low sodium with euvolaemia, not a raised urea and dry membranes.

steps.x: A: Dehydration. Complications of constipation: anal fissure, hypercalcaemia, dehydration.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with long-standing constipation has 2 days of severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and no flatus. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic with tinkling bowel sounds. Rectal examination shows an empty rectum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Vomiting, distension, severe pain and absent flatus in a constipated patient suggest bowel obstruction, which needs urgent assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Constipation plus vomiting and no flatus = obstruction until proven otherwise.

elim: Impaction would give a loaded rectum and no vomiting.
Gastroenteritis causes diarrhoea, not absent flatus and tinkling bowel sounds.
IBS does not cause vomiting, gross distension or tachycardia.
Vomiting, no flatus and tinkling bowel sounds are red flags beyond simple constipation.

steps.x: A: Bowel obstruction. Red flag: vomiting, distension, severe pain, no flatus = urgent surgical assessment.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has had hard stools every 3 days for 2 months since starting a desk job. He has no pain, bleeding, weight loss or family history of bowel cancer. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal. He asks for a test to confirm what is wrong.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Constipation is a clinical diagnosis based on the history and examination; tests are for red flags or suspected secondary causes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: no pain, bleeding, weight loss or family history
steps.x: No red flags and normal examination: no test needed to make the diagnosis.

elim: X-rays do not diagnose constipation and add radiation.
Transit studies are for refractory cases in specialist care.
Colonoscopy is for red flags, which he does not have.
FIT is for suspected cancer, which is not suspected here.

steps.x: B: Clinical history and examination. Gold standard: clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has 6 weeks of new constipation. He feels tired and thirsty. He has no rectal bleeding or weight loss. His abdomen is soft and rectal examination shows soft stool only. He is on no regular medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial set of investigations?
questions.e: New constipation needs basic bloods for secondary causes: FBC (anaemia from occult cancer), TSH (hypothyroidism), calcium (hypercalcaemia) and U&Es.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial set of investigations? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Thirst and tiredness raise hypercalcaemia and anaemia; the basic screen covers both.

elim: An X-ray will not find metabolic or endocrine causes.
Imaging is not the first step without red flags; bloods come first.
LFTs are not part of the basic constipation screen.
CEA is not a diagnostic test.

steps.x: C: FBC, TSH, calcium and U&Es. First-line: FBC, TSH, calcium and U&Es.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has 2 months of constipation and fatigue. She has no visible rectal bleeding. Her GP sends a FIT, which comes back at 42 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Iron supplements and review in 3 months
Start a bulk-forming laxative and review
questions.e: Over 50 with microcytic anaemia is an indication for FIT; a positive FIT warrants colonoscopy via the urgent suspected cancer pathway.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Microcytic anaemia plus positive FIT = urgent colonoscopy.

elim: Treating the anaemia without finding its cause risks missing cancer.
A positive FIT needs investigation now.
Laxatives do not address a possible cancer.
Ultrasound does not image the colonic mucosa.

steps.x: E: Urgent referral for colonoscopy. Red flags warrant urgent colorectal investigation.

questions.stem: A 91 year old woman in a care home has 3 days of brown liquid stool leaking into her pad. Staff say she usually opens her bowels once a week. She is immobile and takes co-codamol. She has no fever and her abdomen is soft. The nurse asks whether to start loperamide.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial examination?
questions.e: Liquid stool in an immobile patient on opioids who usually opens her bowels weekly suggests overflow from faecal impaction; DRE confirms it, and loperamide must be avoided.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial examination? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Diarrhoea in a chronically constipated elderly patient: feel the rectum first.

elim: Ultrasound is not needed to assess stool in the rectum.
This is invasive and not the first step.
Proctoscopy is for anal canal pathology such as haemorrhoids.
Infection is unlikely; impaction must be excluded first, and loperamide would worsen it.

steps.x: B: Digital rectal examination. Overflow diarrhoea is treated as impaction, not as diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 3 day old term baby girl has not passed meconium. She has abdominal distension and has started bilious vomiting. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops. A contrast enema shows a narrow rectum with a dilated colon above it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Hirschsprung's disease is diagnosed by rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells in the affected segment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: narrow rectum with a dilated colon above it
steps.x: Narrow distal segment with dilated bowel above = aganglionosis; prove it histologically.

elim: Manometry may suggest it but biopsy is diagnostic.
CT does not show the absence of ganglion cells.
A sweat test looks for cystic fibrosis (meconium ileus), not Hirschsprung's.
This looks for malrotation, not the aganglionic rectum.

steps.x: C: Rectal suction biopsy. Hirschsprung's: rectal biopsy, absent ganglion cells.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has 3 months of new constipation and 6 kg of weight loss. He has seen dark red blood mixed with his stool twice. His father had bowel cancer. His abdomen is soft and rectal examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Lifestyle advice and review in 6 weeks
questions.e: New constipation with weight loss and rectal bleeding over 50 are red flags for colorectal cancer, a structural secondary cause, and warrant urgent (2-week-wait) investigation with colonoscopy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: dark red blood mixed with his stool
steps.x: Change in habit plus red flags in an older person = 2-week-wait.

elim: Red flags must not be watched.
Weight loss and bleeding over 50 need the 2-week-wait pathway.
Laxatives do not address red flags.
Bloods are part of work-up but cannot replace urgent investigation.

steps.x: E: Urgent suspected cancer referral. Red flags warrant colonoscopy or 2-week-wait referral.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has 2 months of hard stools every 3 days. She works long shifts, eats mostly takeaways, drinks about 1 litre of fluid a day and rarely exercises. She has no red flags and has not tried any treatment. Examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: First-line management of constipation is lifestyle: more fibre, more fluid and more physical activity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Untreated, low fibre, low fluid: fix the lifestyle first.

elim: Osmotic laxatives are second-line after lifestyle and bulk-forming laxatives.
Enemas are for impaction or rectal stimulation, not first-line.
There are no red flags.
Stimulants are second-line.

steps.x: A: Increase fibre, fluids and activity. Lifestyle first, then bulk-forming, then osmotic, then stimulant.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man was started on ispaghula husk for constipation 2 weeks ago after lifestyle measures failed. His stools are now even harder and he feels bloated. He drinks two cups of tea a day and little else. He has no red flags.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Double the ispaghula dose without other change
questions.e: Bulk-forming laxatives work by absorbing water to increase faecal mass; without adequate hydration they harden the stool and can cause obstruction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: two cups of tea a day and little else
steps.x: Bulk laxatives need water to work.

elim: Loperamide is an antidiarrhoeal and would worsen constipation.
More bulk without water worsens the problem.
Fibre helps; the problem is lack of water.
Codeine is an opioid and constipating.

steps.x: C: Increase his fluid intake. Ispaghula husk is the first-line laxative but requires adequate fluid intake.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has constipation. She increased her fibre and fluid intake and has taken ispaghula husk for 6 weeks with plenty of water, but still passes hard stools every 4 days. She has no red flags and her bloods are normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If lifestyle and a bulk-forming laxative fail, the next step is an osmotic laxative: macrogol 1 sachet twice daily (or lactulose 15 ml twice daily).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Bulk-forming failed with hard stools: add water to the stool with an osmotic.

elim: Rectal measures are for establishing a routine or impaction, not the next oral step.
There are no red flags.
Docusate is used mainly for opioid-induced constipation.
Loperamide treats diarrhoea.

steps.x: E: Macrogol. Second-line: osmotic (macrogol, lactulose), then stimulant (senna, bisacodyl).

questions.stem: A 62 year old man takes macrogol twice daily for constipation. His stools are now soft, but he still only opens his bowels every 4 to 5 days and feels he cannot get things moving. He has no red flags and examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Soft but infrequent stools mean motility, not consistency, is the problem; a stimulant laxative such as senna 15 mg at night or bisacodyl increases colonic motility.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Soft but stuck = add a stimulant.

elim: Loperamide slows the bowel further.
Bulk agents are first-line and he needs a push rather than more bulk.
Surgery has no place in uncomplicated constipation.
His stools are soft because of macrogol; keep it.

steps.x: B: Add senna. Osmotic softens; stimulant pushes.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has a complete T6 spinal cord injury from a road traffic collision. He has chronic constipation with episodes of faecal incontinence and does not feel the urge to open his bowels. He takes macrogol daily. The spinal team want to set up a predictable bowel pattern.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to his management?
questions.e: Rectal stimulation (suppositories, enemas or digital stimulation) at a set time helps establish a regular bowel routine, especially in spinal cord disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate addition to his management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
No sensation and need for routine = timed rectal stimulation.

elim: Loperamide would worsen his constipation.
A stoma is a last resort, not the next step.
Fibre alone will not give a predictable routine in neurogenic bowel.
His stools still need softening.

steps.x: D: Regular rectal stimulation. Rectal stimulation establishes a regular routine.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer takes regular modified-release morphine for bone pain. She has hard stools and strains. Her palliative care team want a stool softener and do not want to use bulk-forming agents because she drinks very little.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medicine?
questions.e: Opioid-induced constipation is treated with a stool softener such as docusate sodium, or a stimulant plus osmotic combination such as senna plus macrogol.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate medicine? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Opioid constipation: softener or stimulant plus osmotic, never bulk.

elim: Codeine is another opioid and worsens constipation.
Bulk-forming agents need good fluid intake and are avoided in opioid-induced constipation.
Loperamide is an antidiarrhoeal opioid agonist.
Her pain control matters; treat the side effect instead.

steps.x: B: Docusate sodium. Opioid-induced constipation: docusate, or senna plus macrogol.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl has had hard, painful stools every 4 days for 3 months since starting nursery. She withholds stool and cries on the toilet. She was born at term, passed meconium on day 1 and is growing well. Examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line laxative?
questions.e: First-line laxative for children is macrogol (Movicol Paediatric); lactulose is the next option and senna is added if it is not working.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate first-line laxative? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Normal meconium and growth makes this functional childhood constipation.

elim: Rectal treatment is distressing and not first-line in children.
Docusate is not first-line in children.
Bulk-forming agents are not first-line for childhood constipation.
Enemas are not used first-line in children.

steps.x: D: Macrogol (Movicol Paediatric). Paediatric: Movicol first, then lactulose; add senna if needed.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with chronic constipation on senna has 2 days of severe abdominal pain, vomiting and no flatus. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 104/68 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and tympanic. A nurse suggests a phosphate enema.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nil by mouth, IV fluids and surgical review
questions.e: Vomiting, distension, severe pain and no flatus suggest bowel obstruction: stop laxatives, keep nil by mouth, give IV fluids (with NG decompression) and arrange urgent surgical assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Obstruction: no laxatives, resuscitate and get surgeons.

elim: Stimulant laxatives can perforate an obstructed bowel.
Oral laxatives are contraindicated in suspected obstruction.
Bulk agents worsen obstruction.
This misses a surgical emergency.

steps.x: D: Nil by mouth, IV fluids and surgical review. Red flags of obstruction need urgent assessment, not laxatives.

questions.stem: An 87 year old woman is admitted with faecal impaction. Rectal examination shows a rectum packed with hard stool. She was given one sachet of macrogol yesterday with no result. She has no vomiting and her abdomen is soft.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Faecal impaction is treated with high-dose macrogol plus a rectal enema or suppository to soften and clear the impacted mass.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
One sachet is not impaction dosing; go high-dose and treat from below too.

elim: Bulk agents add to the mass and can worsen impaction.
Loperamide would worsen the impaction.
This is a last resort, not the next step.
A stimulant against a hard impacted mass causes colic without clearing it.

steps.x: A: High-dose macrogol with a suppository. Faecal impaction: high-dose macrogol plus enema or suppository.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has slow-transit constipation confirmed on a colonic marker study. Markers remain spread through the whole colon after 5 days. She asks why her stools are always so hard.
questions.q: Which best explains the hardness of her stools?
o: Prolonged water reabsorption in the colon
questions.e: Slow colonic transit allows prolonged water reabsorption from the stool, producing hard, difficult-to-pass stools.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the hardness of her stools? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: Markers remain spread through the whole colon
steps.x: The longer stool stays, the more water the colon takes out.

elim: Bile acids in the colon cause watery stool.
Mucus would soften rather than harden stool.
Secretion makes stool looser.
This is the opposite: less absorption gives loose stools.

steps.x: D: Prolonged water reabsorption in the colon. Constipation = slow transit and/or defecatory dysfunction; longer contact means harder stool.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is started on oxybutynin for urge incontinence. Three weeks later she has a dry mouth and hard stools every 5 days. She has no other new medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her constipation?
o: Calcium channel blockade in gut smooth muscle
Reduced parasympathetic stimulation of gut smooth muscle
questions.e: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic: blocking acetylcholine reduces parasympathetic stimulation of gut smooth muscle and slows peristalsis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Dry mouth tells you the drug is anticholinergic.

elim: This is how opioids cause constipation.
This is the mechanism for drugs such as amlodipine.
Oxybutynin does not raise calcium.
Oxybutynin does not affect the thyroid.

steps.x: E: Reduced parasympathetic stimulation of gut smooth muscle. Anticholinergics block parasympathetic drive to the gut and slow peristalsis.

questions.stem: A 5 week old boy has had a rectal biopsy for delayed passage of meconium and abdominal distension. Histology confirms Hirschsprung's disease affecting the rectum and sigmoid colon. His parents ask how this happened during pregnancy.
questions.q: Which embryological process has failed?
questions.e: Neural crest cells fail to migrate down to the distal bowel, leaving an aganglionic segment that cannot relax, causing functional obstruction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which embryological process has failed? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Ganglion cells come from neural crest; no migration means no ganglia.

This relates to cystic fibrosis and meconium ileus.

steps.x: C: Neural crest cell migration. Hirschsprung's: failed neural crest migration, aganglionic distal segment, cannot relax.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman is started on ispaghula husk for constipation and told to drink plenty of water with it. She asks how it works.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of this laxative?
o: Absorbs water to increase faecal mass
Blocks opioid receptors in the gut
Draws water into the lumen osmotically
Lubricates and softens via surfactant action
questions.e: Bulk-forming laxatives absorb water to increase faecal mass, which distends the colon and stimulates peristalsis; hence the need for fluid.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of action of this laxative? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Bulk = more mass = stretch = peristalsis.

elim: Peripheral opioid antagonists such as naloxegol work this way.
This is how stimulant laxatives like senna work.
This is how macrogol and lactulose work.
This describes docusate.

steps.x: A: Absorbs water to increase faecal mass. Bulk-forming: mass; osmotic: water into lumen; stimulant: enteric nerves.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with Parkinson's disease takes bisacodyl at night for constipation. He notices crampy lower abdominal pain about 8 hours after each dose, before he opens his bowels.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this laxative?
o: Absorption of water to add bulk
questions.e: Stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl) directly stimulate colonic motility via the enteric nerves; cramping is a typical side effect.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of this laxative? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Cramps after a stimulant reflect increased contractions.

elim: That is how ispaghula husk works.
This is a stool softener effect.
This is how macrogol and lactulose work.
This would harden stool.

steps.x: E: Stimulation of enteric nerves. Stimulant laxatives: enteric nerve stimulation and increased motility.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with constipation takes macrogol (Movicol) 1 sachet twice daily dissolved in water. Her stools become softer within 2 days. She asks why it has to be taken with a glass of water.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of macrogol?
o: Blocks colonic water absorption via chloride channels
Retains water in the bowel lumen osmotically
questions.e: Macrogol is an osmotic laxative: the polymer holds water in the bowel lumen, softening and increasing stool volume.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of action of macrogol? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Osmotic laxatives keep water in the lumen.

elim: Bulk-forming agents like ispaghula work this way.
This is how opioids slow the gut.
This is not the mechanism of macrogol.
That is how stimulant laxatives work.

steps.x: D: Retains water in the bowel lumen osmotically. Osmotic laxatives: macrogol, lactulose; they draw or hold water in the lumen.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man with dementia has a week of leaking loose stool. Rectal examination shows a large mass of hard faeces filling the rectum. His daughter asks how he can have diarrhoea and constipation at the same time.
questions.q: Which best explains his loose stool?
o: Liquid stool leaking around impacted faeces
questions.e: Liquid stool from above leaks around a large impacted faecal mass in the rectum, mimicking diarrhoea; the underlying problem is constipation and impaction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains his loose stool? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: large mass of hard faeces filling the rectum
steps.x: Overflow is constipation in disguise.

elim: He has had no antibiotics and the rectum is impacted.
Stasis does not explain leakage around a hard mass.
Secretion is not the cause of overflow.
The mass is faeces on DRE, not a tumour.

steps.x: D: Liquid stool leaking around impacted faeces. Overflow diarrhoea: treat the impaction.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has 3 months of new constipation, a feeling of incomplete emptying and 5 kg of weight loss. She has never been constipated before. Her abdomen is soft with a vague left iliac fossa fullness that does not indent. Her TSH and calcium are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her constipation?
questions.e: New constipation in an older patient with weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia and a non-indentable mass suggests a structural cause, colorectal cancer, and needs urgent colonoscopy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
New change in habit late in life plus red flags = structural cause.

elim: New constipation over 60 with weight loss and anaemia is not functional until cancer is excluded.
Her calcium is normal.
Her TSH is normal.
IBS does not start at 71 with weight loss and anaemia.

steps.x: A: Colorectal carcinoma. Structural secondary causes: colorectal cancer, stricture.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with angina is started on verapamil. A month later he has hard stools every 4 days and strains. He has no other new medicines, no red flags and normal bloods.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his constipation?
questions.e: Calcium channel blockers reduce calcium entry into intestinal smooth muscle, decreasing motility and slowing colonic transit; verapamil is the worst offender.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his constipation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
CCB = less calcium into smooth muscle = less contraction.

elim: Verapamil is not anticholinergic; that is amitriptyline or oxybutynin.
Verapamil blocks calcium channels; it does not raise serum calcium.
Verapamil does not affect thyroid function.
That is the opioid mechanism.

steps.x: E: Reduced intestinal smooth muscle contraction. CCBs (e.g. amlodipine, verapamil) decrease intestinal motility.
